draft.title: The Battle for Australia
card: On 19 February 1942, Japanese aircraft bombed Darwin. It was the first and largest of many air raids on northern Australia. Darwin was an important base for Allied ships and aircraft.

In 1942, Australian soldiers fought the Japanese along the Kokoda Track, a narrow path over steep mountains in Papua, in New Guinea. The fighting was in thick jungle, with heavy rain, disease and supply problems.
Many Papuan and New Guinean men helped the Australians on the track. They carried supplies and carried the wounded to safety.

Japan was now close to Australia, and Britain could not defend it. Prime Minister John Curtin turned to the United States for help in the Pacific War, and American forces began to base themselves in Australia.
draft.remember: In 1942 Japan attacked Australia's north and Australians fought in New Guinea, so Australia looked to the United States.

a.q: Why did Australia turn to the United States for help in 1942?
opts: Japan was close and Britain could not defend Australia
Japan had already invaded and captured Sydney
Britain had asked the United States to take over Australia
Australian troops had all been defeated in New Guinea
a.why: Japan had bombed Darwin and was fighting in New Guinea, while Britain could not protect Australia. Japan did not capture Sydney, and Australians were still fighting in New Guinea.
a.clue: Think about who could protect Australia once Japan was nearby.

b.q: Tom reads that in 1942 Australians fought on the Kokoda Track. Which description fits this campaign?
opts: Fighting in jungle and mountains in Papua, New Guinea
Fighting in desert country in North Africa
Air raids on a northern Australian port
A siege of a city held by British forces
b.why: The Kokoda Track was a narrow path over steep mountains and jungle in Papua, New Guinea. The air raids describe Darwin, which was a bombing and not a track fought over on foot.
b.clue: Kokoda was fought in New Guinea, not in Australia.

wants.brief: A map of Papua and New Guinea showing the Kokoda Track between Port Moresby and the north coast, with Darwin and northern Australia visible to the south, in open licence.
wants.why: It shows how close the fighting was to Australia and where the track ran.

a.best: Japan was close and Britain could not defend Australia

b.best: Fighting in jungle and mountains in Papua, New Guinea

b.q: Tom's great-grandfather fought on the Kokoda Track in 1942. Which description best fits what he faced there?
opts: Fighting on foot through steep, wet and thick jungle
Tank battles across flat, dry and open desert
Warships firing on each other far out at sea
Bombers attacking a town and its harbour from the air
b.why: The Kokoda Track was a narrow path over steep mountains, so soldiers fought on foot in jungle, rain and disease. Bombers attacking a harbour describes the raids on Darwin, which were from the air, not fighting along a track.
